strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: group-robust classification without bias annotations.
BEO is simple, computationally accessible, and can produce pseudo-group labels usable by multiple group-supervised methods.
The experiments cover vision and language, binary and multi-class tasks, five random seeds, several bias strengths, and comparisons with both supervised and annotation-free baselines.
FG-CCDB reports strong empirical results, particularly on CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10, and generally improves over the closely related CCDB baseline.
The manuscript is organized clearly, and the component-swapping experiments with GroupDRO, DFR, and ground-truth groups are useful.
weaknesses: The central reweighting derivation appears mathematically inconsistent. Equation 3 defines W_ij as a multiplicative factor satisfying W_:,j times P_:,j = q. Consequently, every sample in group (i,j) should receive a factor proportional to W_ij. Equation 4 instead divides this factor by N_ij before using it in WeightedRandomSampler. The resulting sampled group mass is proportional to W_ij, not W_ij P_ij, so it does not produce the claimed marginal q or exact distribution matching. This introduces an additional inverse dependence on group size and can severely over-sample small groups. Because this is the core of FG-CCDB, the claimed theoretical justification is unsupported unless the equations or implementation are substantially corrected and re-evaluated.

The formulation is much narrower than the general annotation-free claim suggests. It assumes the number of bias states equals the number of classes and interprets the predictions of a target-label classifier as bias labels. This effectively requires a one-to-one class-to-bias correspondence and does not naturally handle multiple, non-categorical, unknown-cardinality, or non-bijective spurious attributes.

BEO is closely related to existing hard-example discovery and bias-amplification methods, but its novelty is limited to repeatedly retaining high-confidence examples. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish it empirically from the especially relevant bias-amplification literature or several discovery baselines discussed in related work.

Important design choices are weakly validated: the 10% initial subset, top-50% confidence threshold, three enhancement rounds, and model-selection procedure lack systematic sensitivity analysis. Figure 4 covers only three datasets, provides no uncertainty, and even shows poor minority-group prediction on CelebA despite strong downstream results.

The evaluation omits several relevant pseudo-group discovery and mitigation baselines, reports some prior results without uncertainty, and does not establish matched training budgets despite BEO requiring several auxiliary training runs.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code is provided, and preprocessing, checkpoint selection, exact synthetic-data construction, normalization of sampler weights, and several optimization details are insufficiently specified. The division-by-zero behavior for empty predicted groups is also undefined.

There are reporting inconsistencies. For the same FG-CCDB results, Table 1 gives standard deviations such as 0.52 and 0.24, whereas Table 3 reports 0.005 and 0.006; several claims of statistical superiority therefore cannot be trusted without clarification.

The analysis in Figure 3 does not define how categorical class and bias variables are converted into per-feature correlations, and observational changes in these correlations do not demonstrate removal of spurious information. Overall, the empirical gains are promising, but the central mathematical error and narrow assumptions prevent acceptance in the current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: group robustness when bias annotations are unavailable. The proposed pipeline is simple and applies to image and text classification. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/ea99461b71e748d09ab462346c2e964d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Experiments cover five benchmarks, binary and multiclass settings, several bias strengths, five random seeds, and both supervised and annotation-free baselines.
The reported empirical results are promising, particularly the gains over CCDB on CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10.
The modular experiments combining BEO with GroupDRO/DFR and using ground-truth groups with FG-CCDB are useful attempts to separate the contributions of bias discovery and reweighting.
weaknesses: The central reweighting derivation appears incorrect. Equation 3 defines W_ij=q_i/P_ij, which is already the per-sample multiplier needed for P_ij W_ij=q_i. Equation 4 then divides this quantity by N_ij before passing it to WeightedRandomSampler. Consequently, the sampled group mass is proportional to N_ij w_ij=W_ij, rather than P_ij W_ij=q_i. Thus the implemented weights do not establish the claimed exact class-conditional alignment. The claim that the same equations inherently solve class imbalance is also unsupported. This is a major soundness issue affecting the paper's principal technical contribution.

Equation 1 is presented ambiguously: mutual information is the KL term, whereas the additional sum_y p(y)log p(y) term is negative class entropy. The paper neither derives this combined objective nor rigorously demonstrates that its proposed weighting minimizes both terms.

BEO is a fairly direct confidence-based self-training heuristic: train on 10% of the data, retain the most confident 50% per class, and repeat. Confidence can reflect core-feature ease, class difficulty, calibration, or label noise rather than bias. There is no theoretical justification or convincing failure analysis establishing when predictions recover bias attributes.

The method assumes |S|=|Y| and effectively relies on one dominant, class-aligned bias category per label. It is unclear how it handles unequal cardinalities, several simultaneous attributes, continuous attributes, non-diagonal label-bias relationships, or multiple majority groups. These are common cases in the motivating real-world applications and substantially limit the significance of the claimed general method.

Bias-discovery quality is not compared directly against relevant alternatives such as XRM, GEORGE, or other pseudo-group estimators. Figure 4 only examines selected datasets, and its group-accuracy calculation and any label-permutation matching procedure are insufficiently specified.

Important design choices are weakly validated. There is no reported sensitivity analysis for the 10% split, top-50% selection, number of enhancement stages across all datasets, or handling of empty/tiny predicted groups. The appendix merely asserts robustness to gamma without presenting results. Claims of scalability and negligible overhead also lack runtime, memory, or training-cost measurements.

The empirical reporting contains serious inconsistencies. Identical FG-CCDB means have standard deviations differing by roughly two orders of magnitude between Tables 1/2 and Table 3—for example, Waterbirds worst-group accuracy is reported as 90.56±0.24 in Table 1 but 90.56±0.006 in Table 3, while cCIFAR10 at 5% is 78.06±0.30 versus 78.06±0.007. This undermines confidence in the statistical results and reproducibility.

Several analyses are too underspecified to support their interpretation. Figure 3 does not define the correlation statistic for categorical class/bias variables, the analyzed representation, or uncertainty. Baseline results mix values with and without variances and do not clearly distinguish reproduced results from literature values. No code or sufficiently complete implementation protocol is supplied.

Because the work explicitly motivates high-stakes fairness applications and evaluates demographic groups, the lack of an ethical discussion is concerning. Incorrect pseudo-groups could conceal harms or amplify stereotypes, yet the paper does not study this risk or caution against interpreting model-derived clusters as genuine demographic attributes.

Overall, the promising empirical pattern is insufficient to overcome the apparent error in the core weighting formulation, restrictive assumptions, incomplete validation, and inconsistent numerical reporting. The paper is therefore not competitive for acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem: group-robust classification without training or validation bias annotations. The proposed BEO procedure is simple, intuitive, and broadly compatible with existing group-aware methods. Source reviewed: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/59a215343133417ea7e7b5271bedf72e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.

The empirical results are promising. FG-CCDB is competitive with the best annotation-free methods on Waterbirds, CelebA, and CivilComments, while producing substantial improvements over CCDB on cMNIST and cCIFAR10 across multiple bias-conflicting ratios.

Experiments cover five datasets, binary and multiclass settings, image and text modalities, and five random seeds. The BEO repetition study and integrations with GroupDRO and DFR provide useful evidence that the inferred groups contain meaningful bias information.
The method is operationally attractive: group-level weights have low storage overhead, require no iterative weight optimization, and can be used through standard weighted sampling.
weaknesses: There appears to be a consequential inconsistency in the central weighting derivation. Equation 3 defines W=q/P as a multiplicative correction to the original conditional group probabilities, in which case each sample in group (i,j) should receive a weight proportional to W_ij. Equation 4 instead assigns W_ij/N_ij to each sample. Under WeightedRandomSampler, the resulting total mass of that group is W_ij rather than W_ij P_ij, so the claimed identity W_:,j⊙P_:,j=q no longer describes the sampled distribution. The paper should correct or clarify this derivation and empirically verify the actual post-weighting distributions.

The contribution is narrower than suggested by the general group-robust framing. BEO assumes |Y|=|S| and essentially a one-to-one dominant bias/class correspondence. It is unclear how the approach handles multiple independent attributes, unequal numbers of classes and bias values, continuous attributes, multiple majority groups per class, or non-diagonal correlations. The reported weakness on CivilComments illustrates this limitation.

The ablations do not isolate whether the proposed FG-CCDB weighting is better than straightforward group balancing using exactly the same BEO pseudo-groups and training pipeline. Comparisons to GroupDRO-BEO and DFR-BEO change the downstream optimization method, while FG-CCDB-sup changes the group annotations. A direct weighting-rule ablation is needed to substantiate the claimed advantage of fine-grained distribution matching.

Several important design choices receive insufficient analysis, including selecting the top 50%, training BEO on 10% of the data, robustness to pseudo-group errors, empty or extremely small inferred groups, and the computation added by three repeated bias-enhancement stages. The appendix asserts insensitivity to gamma but provides no supporting results.

Reproducibility and reporting need improvement. No code is identified; some implementation details are ambiguous; baseline numbers mix newly run and externally reported results without clear separation; and standard deviations for the same FG-CCDB results disagree sharply between Tables 1/2 and Table 3—for example, 90.56±0.24 versus 90.56±0.006 on Waterbirds. Numerous typographical errors further reduce polish. Overall, the strong empirical signal is encouraging, but the weighting inconsistency and missing controlled baseline currently place the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: annotation-free robustness to spurious correlations. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/469dca2fe71c459082e7204d526fae65/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The proposed pipeline is computationally lightweight, and mode-level weights avoid the feature-storage and iterative weight-optimization costs attributed to CCDB.
The evaluation covers binary, multiclass, and multi-shortcut settings, including five-seed results for the proposed method and useful diagnostics of minority-mode recovery.
The experiments directly examine MST through precision, recall, F1, iteration-count, and hyperparameter analyses. Integrating MST with GroupDRO and DFR is also informative.
FG-CCDB reports substantial improvements over CCDB on CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10.
weaknesses: The central weighting derivation appears mathematically inconsistent. Equation 3 defines a mode multiplier W_ij=q_i/P_ij such that W_:j multiplied elementwise by P_:j equals q. Consequently, each example in mode (i,j) should receive multiplier W_ij if this is the intended reweighted conditional distribution. Equation 4 instead assigns W_ij/M_ij to every example, making the aggregate mass of the mode W_ij rather than q_i. Since P_ij=M_ij/n_j, this produces aggregate mass q_i n_j/M_ij, which generally neither matches q nor minimizes the stated mutual-information objective. The claim that Equation 4 also balances classes is likewise unsupported. This undermines the main theoretical interpretation of FG-CCDB, even if the resulting heuristic empirically works.

The formulation does not address empty confusion cells, for which P_ij=0 makes Equation 3 undefined. Sparse cells are especially likely in the extreme-bias experiments. No smoothing, clipping, normalization, or implementation-level treatment is documented, despite reported weight ratios around 1000 and modes containing as few as 19 examples.

MST does not identify bias attributes in general; it partitions examples using the predicted class of an intentionally biased classifier. The assertion that any accuracy below 100% implies that harmful bias has been captured is false: errors can result from label noise, insufficient capacity, optimization failure, or intrinsically difficult core examples. The equal-opportunity discussion is circular because the proposed bias variable is itself defined from model predictions.

The novelty is moderate. MST closely resembles repeated error/confidence-based bias amplification, while FG-CCDB is a closed-form reweighting over confusion cells. The paper does not adequately distinguish the method conceptually from iterative JTT-style selection, hard-example reweighting, or ordinary group resampling beyond its disputed distribution-matching interpretation.

Claims about handling multiple shortcuts are stronger than the evidence. A C-valued predicted-label variable collapses potentially many shortcut configurations into only C states and cannot generally represent their joint structure. Evaluation is limited to UrbanCars, where DDB has a much smaller combined-shortcut gap, several comparisons lack worst-group accuracy, and no controlled study varies the number or interaction of shortcuts.

Baseline evidence is uneven: many values are imported without uncertainty, some cells are missing, and it is unclear that all methods use identical architectures, selection criteria, preprocessing, and splits. There are no paired significance tests. On Waterbirds, FG-CCDB and CCDB are effectively tied, and several supervised or validation-supervised baselines remain stronger.

The ablation does not isolate the questionable extra inverse-frequency factor in Equation 4. Essential comparisons would include weights W_ij, q_i/M_ij, inverse-mode-frequency balancing, and the stated W_ij/M_ij rule. Without these, the results cannot establish that class-conditional distribution matching—rather than aggressive minority oversampling—causes the gains.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript shows an empty “Code:” field, omits several implementation details, and contains a long appendix written as reviewer-response notes (“R1W1,” “R2W4,” and similar), reducing polish and making the final scientific presentation difficult to follow.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: group robustness without explicit bias annotations. The proposed pipeline is simple and potentially inexpensive relative to methods requiring generative models or extensive group labels.
The empirical study covers binary, multi-class, image, text, single-shortcut, and multi-shortcut benchmarks, generally uses five seeds, and reports substantial gains over CCDB on several settings.

The paper evaluates the quality of the inferred partitions using precision, recall, and F1, and includes useful component ablations by combining MST with GroupDRO/DFR and FG-CCDB with ground-truth annotations.
weaknesses: The central weighting derivation appears mathematically incorrect. Equation 3 defines W_ij=q_i/P_ij as a multiplicative correction satisfying W_:,j⊙P_:,j=q. If every sample in cell (i,j) receives this multiplier, its sample weight should be proportional to W_ij. Equation 4 instead divides by the cell count M_ij. Under WeightedRandomSampler, the resulting cell mass is W_ij, not q_i; since P_ij=M_ij/n_j, the effective sample weight is proportional to q_i n_j/M_ij^2. Thus the implemented sampler does not perform the claimed distribution matching or establish the stated minimization of Equation 1. The empirical method may amount to aggressive inverse-squared cell-frequency weighting, but that is a materially different method.

The formulation is undefined when a confusion cell is empty because P_ij=0 causes division by zero. Empty or extremely small cells are plausible in exactly the highly biased and multi-class regimes emphasized by the paper. No smoothing, clipping, normalization, or numerical treatment is specified, while the acknowledged weight ratios of roughly 1000 suggest instability is consequential.

The claimed ability to represent multiple shortcuts is not supported by the model structure. The inferred bias variable has only C values and is simply the auxiliary classifier's predicted target class. For binary UrbanCars, this produces only two inferred modes per target class and cannot distinguish the four combinations of two binary shortcuts. Showing that one collapsed predicted minority mode contains examples from several ground-truth groups does not demonstrate recovery of the full multi-shortcut structure.

The justification for MST is substantially overstated. An auxiliary model having accuracy below 100% does not imply that its errors encode harmful spurious attributes; errors may arise from label noise, intrinsic difficulty, underfitting, or multiple unrelated factors. The appendix's Equal Opportunity argument defines s using the model's own predictions, making the observed TPR discrepancy largely tautological rather than evidence that an external bias variable was recovered.

The annotation-free claim is weakened by development choices informed by ground-truth groups. The choices of γ, β, and repetition count are justified using minority-mode recall/F1 and known bias-aligned ratios. Sensitivity of final debiased performance to β is not reported, so it is unclear whether the fixed setting transfers without group labels.

The evaluation does not rescue the central soundness issue. Several baseline entries lack variances or are absent, there are no significance tests, and protocol consistency for imported results is insufficiently documented. UrbanCars hyperparameters are omitted from the main optimization table, the code link is blank, and important implementation details needed to reproduce the extreme weights are missing.

The appendix contains extensive rebuttal-style text such as reviewer identifiers and statements that results 'may have been overlooked.' This material does not provide a clean, self-contained technical appendix and repeatedly substitutes assertions for formal analysis. Overall, the promising benchmark results are insufficient to support acceptance because the paper's principal distribution-matching claim conflicts with its own sampling equations.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving group robustness without requiring bias annotations.

The evaluation is broad, covering image and text data, binary and multiclass tasks, single and multiple shortcuts, and several bias-conflict ratios. The strongest gains over CCDB on CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10 are substantial.

MST is evaluated directly through minority-mode precision, recall, and F1, repetition studies, and substitution for annotations in GroupDRO and DFR. This provides more diagnostic evidence than downstream accuracy alone.
The approach is conceptually simple and operationally appealing: confusion-cell statistics enable closed-form weights with low storage requirements, and most reported results use five random seeds.
The paper includes useful ablations of MST versus FG-CCDB, sensitivity analyses for the selection fractions, convergence experiments, and runtime information.
weaknesses: The central weighting derivation is internally inconsistent. Equation 3 defines W_ij=q_i/P_ij as the per-mode multiplicative factor satisfying W_:j⊙P_:j=q. For weighted sampling, every sample in that mode should therefore receive a weight proportional to W_ij. Equation 4 instead assigns W_ij/M_ij. Consequently, the sampled mass of a mode is proportional to M_ij(W_ij/M_ij)=W_ij=q_i/P_ij, not q_i; the resulting conditional distribution is proportional to q_i/P_ij rather than q_i. Thus the implemented weighting does not establish the claimed exact distribution matching or mutual-information minimization. No experiment evaluates the mathematically consistent alternative.

The appendix's purported theoretical justification for MST is not valid. An overfitted model having accuracy below 100% does not imply that its errors reliably identify harmful spurious cues: errors can arise from underfitting, intrinsic ambiguity, label noise, or rare core-feature patterns. Defining the bias variable using the model's own prediction makes the subsequent equal-opportunity argument circular rather than a guarantee.

The C-valued predicted label is a restrictive representation of bias. Multiple distinct shortcuts or shortcut combinations can induce the same predicted class and are then collapsed into one cell. UrbanCars provides encouraging evidence for one two-shortcut setting, but does not substantiate the broader claim that MST recovers the full structure of complex or entangled biases.

The method is undefined when a confusion cell is empty because P_ij=0 causes division by zero. This is especially relevant under extreme imbalance and multiclass prediction. The paper gives no smoothing, clipping, normalization, or numerical-stability procedure, and does not analyze sensitivity to extremely large weights.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the front-page code field is blank, the algorithm does not specify how the three repeated bias-enhancement stages are instantiated, and important sampler details are absent. The appendix also contains rebuttal-style text and references to reviewer identifiers, suggesting that the manuscript was not fully cleaned for submission.

Baseline reporting is uneven: several values lack variances, many appear imported rather than reproduced under one controlled protocol, and the paper provides no significance analysis. Some claimed improvements, such as the Waterbirds WGA gain over CCDB, are smaller than the reported variability.

The empirical results are promising, but because the central distribution-matching interpretation is contradicted by the stated algorithm, they currently support an aggressive rare-cell reweighting heuristic rather than the paper's main technical claim. Resolving this would require correcting the derivation and re-running the key comparisons.
